lessons.title: FTSE 100, DAX, CAC 40, and STOXX 600: What Europe's Indices Tell You

children.text: In 2025, Germany's DAX rose 23.01% and London's FTSE 100 gained 21.51%, its best year since 2009. Both beat the S&P 500 and left the Nifty 50, up about 10.5%, far behind. On 2 January 2026, the FTSE 100 crossed 10,000 for the first time. Headlines declared that Europe was back. But look closer. The DAX figure includes reinvested dividends, while the others do not. And the FTSE 100's rally had surprisingly little to do with the British economy, because most of its companies earn their money outside Britain. European indices can tell you a lot, as long as you know what each one is actually measuring.

body.text: A European index tells you about the companies inside it, not the country on its label. Before reading any move, check three things: the sector mix, where the companies earn their revenue, and whether dividends are included.

This chart is not a fair race. The DAX is a performance index that reinvests dividends, while the FTSE 100, CAC 40, STOXX 600, S&P 500 and Nifty 50 figures are price returns only. Each is also measured in its own currency. Comparing them directly is like comparing a runner's time with a wind-assisted sprinter's. You will learn to adjust for both in this lesson.

children.text: The FTSE 100: A Global Index With a London Address

markDefs.definition: The index of the 101st to 350th largest London-listed companies. Its members earn a much larger share of revenue inside the UK, so it tracks the British economy more closely than the FTSE 100.

children.text: The FTSE 100 is packed with oil majors like Shell and BP, miners like Rio Tinto and Glencore, drugmakers like AstraZeneca and GSK, banks like HSBC and consumer giants like Unilever. Research by Capital Group found that around three-quarters of FTSE 100 revenue comes from outside the UK, much of it in US dollars. That makes the index a play on global commodity prices, global healthcare and the dollar, not on British shoppers. If you want the UK economy, look at the

body.caption: Why a weaker pound lifts the reported profits of dollar-earning FTSE 100 companies

body.title: The weak pound bonus
body.prompt: A FTSE 100 oil company earns a profit of $10 billion. GBP/USD falls from 1.35 to 1.25, meaning the pound weakens. With the same dollar profit, by what percentage does its profit in pounds rise? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: At 1.35: $10 billion ÷ 1.35 = £7.41 billion. At 1.25: $10 billion ÷ 1.25 = £8.00 billion. Increase = (8.00 ÷ 7.41 − 1) × 100 = 8.0%. The company did not sell a single extra barrel, yet its sterling profit rose 8%. The same thing happens to TCS and Infosys when the rupee weakens against the dollar.

body.title: Bad news for Britain
body.question: Weak UK economic data sends the pound sharply lower against the dollar. What is the most likely reaction?
options: Both the FTSE 100 and FTSE 250 fall by about the same amount
The FTSE 100 holds up better than the FTSE 250, because its companies earn mostly in foreign currencies
The FTSE 250 rises because domestic companies benefit from a weak pound
Neither index reacts, since currencies do not affect share prices
body.explanation: FTSE 100 companies earn about three-quarters of their revenue abroad, so a weaker pound raises the sterling value of those earnings and cushions the index. FTSE 250 companies depend more on the UK economy, so weak domestic data hits them harder. This is why the two indices can move in opposite directions on the same day.

children.text: The DAX: Germany's Index With Dividends Built In

markDefs.definition: An index that assumes all dividends are reinvested back into the index. Also called a total return index. The Nifty 50 TRI is India's version; the regular Nifty 50 is a price index.

children.text: The DAX tracks the 40 largest German companies by free-float market cap, led by SAP and Siemens, which together make up about a fifth of the index. It expanded from 30 to 40 stocks in September 2021. Its unusual feature is that the headline DAX is a

: dividends are assumed to be reinvested. Almost every other headline index, including the Nifty 50, S&P 500, FTSE 100 and CAC 40, ignores dividends. So over long periods, the DAX gets a built-in head start of a few percentage points a year. Indian investors already know this idea: since 2018, SEBI has required mutual funds to benchmark against Total Return Indices like the Nifty 50 TRI.

body.caption: A quick approximation for stripping dividends out of a performance index

body.title: Put the DAX on a level field
body.prompt: The DAX returned 23.01% in 2025, including reinvested dividends. Assume the DAX companies paid an average dividend yield of about 2.7% during the year. Using the approximation above, what was the DAX's approximate price return, in percent? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Price return ≈ 23.01% − 2.7% = 20.31%. The 2.7% yield is an illustrative assumption, not official data. On a price-only basis, the DAX's lead over the FTSE 100's 21.51% disappears. Before comparing any two indices, make sure both are price indices or both are total return indices.

children.text: The CAC 40: Energy, Industry and Luxury

France's CAC 40 is a price index of 40 large companies on Euronext Paris. Its heaviest weights are an oil major, an electrical equipment giant and a cluster of luxury and beauty houses whose customers are wealthy shoppers in China, the US and the Middle East. That is why the CAC 40 often reacts more to Chinese consumer data than to French GDP. In 2025 it lagged its neighbours, rising only 10.42%, as French political instability and a slowdown in luxury spending weighed on the index.

body.text: Hermès is one of the most valuable companies in France, yet its CAC 40 weight is under 3%. The reason is free float. The founding family controls most of its shares, so only a small portion is available to trade. It is the same logic that gives some promoter-heavy Indian companies a smaller Nifty weight than their total market cap suggests.

children.text: STOXX 600 and EURO STOXX 50: Europe as One Market

Global fund managers rarely think in terms of Germany or France alone. They use pan-European benchmarks run by STOXX, part of Deutsche Börse Group. The STOXX Europe 600 is the broad measure of European equities, and the one most often quoted when news reports say "European stocks rose". The EURO STOXX 50 is narrower: 50 blue chips from countries that use the euro. That single rule changes the membership dramatically.

columns.label: STOXX Europe 600
points: 17 countries, including non-euro markets like the UK, Switzerland, Sweden and Denmark
Includes Nestlé, Roche, AstraZeneca, Shell and Novo Nordisk
The best single gauge of European equities

columns.label: EURO STOXX 50
points: Includes ASML, SAP, LVMH, Siemens and TotalEnergies
Excludes UK, Swiss and Danish giants
Widely used for futures, options and ETFs

body.title: Who qualifies for the EURO STOXX 50?
body.question: Which of these companies can be a member of the EURO STOXX 50?
body.explanation: The EURO STOXX 50 only includes companies from eurozone countries. The Netherlands uses the euro, so ASML qualifies. Switzerland uses the Swiss franc, the UK uses the pound and Denmark uses the Danish krone, so Nestlé, AstraZeneca and Novo Nordisk are excluded, although all three are in the broader STOXX Europe 600.

children.text: What Your Return Looks Like in Rupees

Index returns are quoted in local currency. An Indian investor earns the index return and the currency move together. If the euro strengthens against the rupee, your rupee return is higher than the headline. If it weakens, your return shrinks. The two effects multiply, they do not simply add.

body.caption: Combining a local-currency index return with the currency move against the rupee

body.title: A DAX return in rupees
body.prompt: Illustrative figures: a DAX-tracking investment returns 23% in euros over a year, and the euro strengthens 12% against the rupee over the same period. What is the return in rupees, in percent? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Return in ₹ = (1 + 0.23) × (1 + 0.12) − 1 = 1.23 × 1.12 − 1 = 1.3776 − 1 = 37.76%. Simply adding 23% and 12% gives 35%, which understates the result. The currency move is not a side detail. It can be as large as the equity return itself, in either direction.

body.title: Spot the odd index
body.textWithBlank: Unlike the FTSE 100 and CAC 40, Germany's headline ___ index includes reinvested dividends.
body.explanation: The headline DAX is a performance index, so it assumes dividends are reinvested. The FTSE 100 and CAC 40 are price indices. Always check before comparing returns.

body.title: Decode a European market close
body.scenario: At 9:15 pm IST, a business channel reports: "European markets closed mixed. The DAX rose 1.4%, the CAC 40 added 0.3% and the FTSE 100 slipped 0.5%. Brent crude fell 4% and the pound jumped 1.2% against the dollar after stronger UK wage data. Chinese retail sales disappointed."
body.prompt: Explain why each index most likely moved the way it did, using what you know about their sector mix and revenue sources.
body.modelAnswer:
1. FTSE 100 down 0.5%: Two headwinds hit it at once. A 4% fall in Brent crude hurts heavyweights like Shell and BP. And a stronger pound reduces the sterling value of the dollar earnings that make up most FTSE 100 revenue.
2. CAC 40 up only 0.3%: TotalEnergies, its largest weight, would be dragged down by falling oil. Disappointing Chinese retail sales are bad news for LVMH, L'Oréal and Hermès. Other sectors, such as industrials, likely offset this, leaving a small gain.
3. DAX up 1.4%: The DAX has little direct oil exposure and is led by software, industrials and financials. Cheaper oil lowers costs for German manufacturers. Also remember the DAX includes dividends, though that does not affect a single day's move much.
4. The lesson: the same evening can look bullish or bearish depending on which index you watch. The sector mix, not the country, explains the split.

body.title: Read any European index headline properly
steps: Identify the index and check its top five weights and largest sectors.
Ask where its companies earn revenue: domestic, dollar-based or global.
Check whether it is a price index or a performance index before comparing returns.
Note the currency move: pound or euro against the dollar, and against the rupee if you invest.
Match the move to that day's news on oil, China, interest rates or currencies.

points: In 2025, the DAX rose 23.01%, the FTSE 100 21.51%, the STOXX Europe 600 16.67% and the CAC 40 10.42%, compared with about 16% for the S&P 500 and 10.5% for the Nifty 50.
The FTSE 100 earns about 77% of its revenue outside the UK, so a weaker pound tends to lift it. The FTSE 250 is a better gauge of the UK economy.
The headline DAX includes reinvested dividends, unlike most other indices. Subtract the dividend yield to compare it fairly.
The CAC 40 is driven by energy, industrials and luxury and beauty, so it often reacts to oil prices and Chinese consumers.
The STOXX Europe 600 covers 17 countries including the UK and Switzerland. The EURO STOXX 50 covers eurozone blue chips only.
Free float matters in Europe as in India. Family-controlled Hermès has a CAC 40 weight under 3%.
In rupees, returns compound with currency moves: (1 + index return) × (1 + currency change) − 1.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Index returns, weights and composition are drawn from FactSet, Euronext, STOXX, Capital Group research and published reports as of the dates stated, and may change. Dividend yield and currency figures in the exercises are illustrative. Companies and indices named are examples, not recommendations.
